answer.rationale: The degradation is region-confined, which points at a regional cause rather than the release itself, and rollback is foreclosed anyway by the compliance ruling on the security patch (so memory_b1's rollback success is inapplicable here regardless of how well it worked on day 18). Capacity and read-replica routing (memory_b3, memory_b5) address the wrong failure shape: this is write-path p99 in one region, not aggregate saturation or read contention on the primary. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) fail fast, which sheds exactly the settlement writes we are told not to lose. That leaves regional failover as the only candidate whose mechanism matches the observed locality. But memory_b2 is the single memory my choice rests on, and its summary is silent on the two things that matter most at day 74: whether the March degradation involved heavy writes, and whether the 'clean' traffic shift was verified against replication lag. A failover that cuts over ahead of replication during peak settlement writes is precisely how you lose customer writes while the latency graph looks like it recovered. So I am spending the one verification pull on memory_b2 to read the original record for write volume and any lag or reconciliation notes. Pending that, I intend a small guarded shift: move a thin slice of write traffic with replication lag as a hard gate and an abort if lag grows, rather than a full cutover. If the archived record shows March was read-dominated or that lag was never checked, the memory does not transfer and I hold at the guarded slice instead of widening. Uncertainty remains real: the 90-minute climb could also be an interaction between the new build and peak write load that happens to present as regional, which failover would carry with it rather than cure.
